physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. The city is divided into districts, each with its unique characteristics, such as the Industrial Quarter, the Residential Loop, and the Sovereign's Circle.
races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Sovereigns live in the opulent Sovereign's Circle, while the rest of the population resides in the ever-changing districts. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. The Verdant Folk live in harmony with nature in the Verdant Expanse, while the Crystal Dwarves mine moonstones in the Crystal Peaks. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.


## Story Details
title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. Your landlord, old Grenn, has left a note under your door demanding the overdue rent by morning, or he'll have your table and your instruments out in the lane by noon. The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.
summary: The player is a cartographer hired by the Lunar Sovereigns to map the nightly rearrangements of the city of Nocturnis, where buildings, streets, and landmarks shift with the moon's phases due to residual magical energy called Nocturna. As they work, they uncover conspiracies within the Sovereigns, encounter the displaced peoples of the Scorch Nomads and Verdant Folk, and grapple with the disorienting effects of prolonged exposure to Nocturna, which causes memory loss. The game's tone is grounded, atmospheric, and focused on mystery and survival in a world that refuses to stay still.


## The Place
name: Larkspur Quarter rooftops
teaser: Climb higher and watch the city read itself into a new shape tonight.

## Instructions
Write this place out in full.
- The description is what the player reads on arrival. Address them as "you"
- Describe what is here now, not the history -- the history is the lore
- Stay consistent with the universe and with the teaser above
- Respect the stated length of each field

## What Is Lying Here
List AT MOST 3 portable things a player could pick up and carry away.
- Nothing is the right answer for most rooms. An empty list is a complete answer
- Only loose, portable things. Not the door, not the floor, not the machinery
  bolted to it -- something a person could put in a pocket or under an arm
- Each one must be consistent with the description you just wrote, and worth
  the player noticing
- Pick its use_kind from the supplied physical profiles. Ordinary is the
  default. Food and drink can be consumed without healing; healing is only
  a restorative dose this world permits. Firestarters burn combustible
  objects, levers pry jammed passages, lockpicks try locks, and a key only
  opens a passage explicitly matched to it. Mark combustible only when an
  ordinary firestarter can destroy the object. The engine owns the effects
  and their amounts; its description cannot grant extra powers
- If a thing has WRITING on it -- a note, a letter, a handbill, a label, a
  docket, a page, a sign -- mark it readable and WRITE OUT WHAT IS WRITTEN
  ON IT, exactly as it appears on the thing. The words themselves, not a
  description of them, and short enough to finish -- a few words, a line,
  or a few short lines. The game keeps those words and a player reading it
  twice reads the same ones
- Never name it after a person or after a place. Already spoken for in this story, so do not reuse: Isbet Marrow, Grenn Ollivar, Marek Sollen, bell-rope tally

## Who Is Here
Write NOBODY into this place. There is nobody here, and the description
should read like somewhere nobody is standing.

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: People who are in this place right now.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

unconscious_desire.description: What they are actually pursuing and would deny if you said it to them. It sits at an angle to the conscious desire rather than agreeing with it: the conscious desire is the reason they give themselves, and this is what keeps them going when that reason runs out. One sentence, third person, by name.

recognized_need.description: Something they know they must do whether they want to or not, and may resent. A real obligation this world imposes on them -- their work, their family, their debt, their oath, their body -- and one that can get in the way of the conscious desire. One sentence, third person, by name.

unrecognized_need.description: What they need and cannot see, not even unconsciously. A reader should be able to see it from the backstory above while they cannot. If they never do it, pursuing the conscious desire ruins them. It must not be the conscious desire said twice. One sentence, third person, by name.

desire_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the CONSCIOUS DESIRE has -- the one that fits the act they would take tomorrow morning.

need_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the UNRECOGNIZED NEED has. It may be the same label as the one above; the more interesting answer is usually a different one.

You build the rooms of a text adventure one at a time. You write places a
player can stand in and walk out of: concrete, specific, and consistent
with the world they belong to. Every exit you name is somewhere the player
could actually go.

DO NOT INCLUDE EMOJIS IN YOUR RESPONSE.

- One way out is a complete answer. A dead end, a cell, the bottom of a
  shaft: if the only way out is back the place the player came from, list

  workshop, a shrine somebody keeps -- somewhere with a reason for

  anybody there: a cellar, a back stair, a stretch of road, a room that is

exits.description: The places a player can reach directly from here.

teaser.description: A one-line glimpse of what lies that way, enough to make the player choose it. Exactly one sentence.

distance.description: How far it is. Pick the closest of these; the exact wording does not matter.

travel_method.description: How the player covers that ground. Pick the closest of these. It must read correctly in both directions, because the way back is the same edge.

inside.description: NO INSIDE for almost everything you name. population.description: How many people are in that place. Pick the closest of these words. It is a word and never a number: the engine decides how many people that is.

## Universe Details
physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. The city is divided into districts, each with its unique characteristics, such as the Industrial Quarter, the Residential Loop, and the Sovereign's Circle.
races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Sovereigns live in the opulent Sovereign's Circle, while the rest of the population resides in the ever-changing districts. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. The Verdant Folk live in harmony with nature in the Verdant Expanse, while the Crystal Dwarves mine moonstones in the Crystal Peaks. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.


## Story Details
title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. Your landlord, old Grenn, has left a note under your door demanding the overdue rent by morning, or he'll have your table and your instruments out in the lane by noon. The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.
summary: The player is a cartographer hired by the Lunar Sovereigns to map the nightly rearrangements of the city of Nocturnis, where buildings, streets, and landmarks shift with the moon's phases due to residual magical energy called Nocturna. As they work, they uncover conspiracies within the Sovereigns, encounter the displaced peoples of the Scorch Nomads and Verdant Folk, and grapple with the disorienting effects of prolonged exposure to Nocturna, which causes memory loss. The game's tone is grounded, atmospheric, and focused on mystery and survival in a world that refuses to stay still.

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: The 2 people who are in this place right now. Write all 2 the instructions describe, in the order they are given there.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

unconscious_desire.description: What they are actually pursuing and would deny if you said it to them. It sits at an angle to the conscious desire rather than agreeing with it: the conscious desire is the reason they give themselves, and this is what keeps them going when that reason runs out. One sentence, third person, by name.

recognized_need.description: Something they know they must do whether they want to or not, and may resent. A real obligation this world imposes on them -- their work, their family, their debt, their oath, their body -- and one that can get in the way of the conscious desire. One sentence, third person, by name.

unrecognized_need.description: What they need and cannot see, not even unconsciously. A reader should be able to see it from the backstory above while they cannot. If they never do it, pursuing the conscious desire ruins them. It must not be the conscious desire said twice. One sentence, third person, by name.

desire_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the CONSCIOUS DESIRE has -- the one that fits the act they would take tomorrow morning.

need_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the UNRECOGNIZED NEED has. It may be the same label as the one above; the more interesting answer is usually a different one.

history.content:
## Universe Details
physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. The city is divided into districts, each with its unique characteristics, such as the Industrial Quarter, the Residential Loop, and the Sovereign's Circle.
races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Sovereigns live in the opulent Sovereign's Circle, while the rest of the population resides in the ever-changing districts. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. The Verdant Folk live in harmony with nature in the Verdant Expanse, while the Crystal Dwarves mine moonstones in the Crystal Peaks. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.


## Story Details
title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. Your landlord, old Grenn, has left a note under your door demanding the overdue rent by morning, or he'll have your table and your instruments out in the lane by noon. The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.

## Universe Details
physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. The city is divided into districts, each with its unique characteristics, such as the Industrial Quarter, the Residential Loop, and the Sovereign's Circle.
races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Sovereigns live in the opulent Sovereign's Circle, while the rest of the population resides in the ever-changing districts. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. The Verdant Folk live in harmony with nature in the Verdant Expanse, while the Crystal Dwarves mine moonstones in the Crystal Peaks. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.


## Story Details
title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. Your landlord, old Grenn, has left a note under your door demanding the overdue rent by morning, or he'll have your table and your instruments out in the lane by noon. The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.
summary: The player is a cartographer hired by the Lunar Sovereigns to map the nightly rearrangements of the city of Nocturnis, where buildings, streets, and landmarks shift with the moon's phases due to residual magical energy called Nocturna. As they work, they uncover conspiracies within the Sovereigns, encounter the displaced peoples of the Scorch Nomads and Verdant Folk, and grapple with the disorienting effects of prolonged exposure to Nocturna, which causes memory loss. The game's tone is grounded, atmospheric, and focused on mystery and survival in a world that refuses to stay still.

  obtain   They are trying to get hold of something they do not have.
  reach    They are trying to get to a particular place.
  attend   They are trying to stay near a particular person.

## Universe Details
physics: Gravity is consistent at 9.8 m/s², but the world is veined with ley lines—thin, invisible rivers of latent magic that pulse at a frequency of 0.3 Hz, detectable only by iron-forged compasses. These lines can be tapped by blood rituals, but each use drains the caster’s lifespan by exactly one day per minute of magic. The ley lines are finite; overuse in a region causes them to fade for a century. No magic can resurrect the dead or heal mortal wounds, only delay them.
technology: The world is locked in a late medieval stasis, with iron and steel as the primary metals. Clockwork mechanisms exist but are rare, limited to devices no larger than a loaf of bread due to the scarcity of precision gears. Gunpowder is known but unstable, often exploding prematurely in 1 out of 5 attempts. Most advancements are suppressed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre, which burns any invention deemed heretical.
geographies: The kingdom of Durnhold is a land of jagged iron cliffs and black pine forests, its heart dominated by the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano where the Church burns heretics. The goblin caves lie beneath the Spire’s roots, a labyrinth of obsidian tunnels lit by bioluminescent fungi that dim every 12 hours. The nearest town, Hollow’s End, is a day’s ride north, its walls built from the bones of ancient trolls. The river Veyth, wide and slow, marks the border between Durnhold and the goblin territories, its waters undrinkable due to high iron content.
races: Durnish, Goblins, Trollkin, Veythi
civilizations: The Kingdom of Durnhold is ruled by the Iron Council, a cabal of knights and priests who enforce the Church’s decrees from the Obsidian Throne in the capital, Spire’s Rest. The goblins are divided into warring clans, the largest being the Blackfang, who control the dungeon where the prince is held. The Trollkin have no settlements, only nomadic bands, while the Veythi operate from floating barges on the river, their only permanent structure being the Rust Market, a black-market hub hidden in the river’s mist. The uneasy peace is maintained by the Iron Council’s threat of annihilation and the goblins’ fear of open war, but raids and executions are common.

title: The Iron Gate Descends
genre: dark fantasy

The prince’s signet ring, cold in your palm, was found in the mud outside this gate—proof he passed this way. Behind you, the tunnel slopes upward, but the way forward is a yawning maw of obsidian, the walls slick with moisture. Somewhere in the dark, something skitters.

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: The person who is in this place right now. Write the one the instructions describe.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

unconscious_desire.description: What they are actually pursuing and would deny if you said it to them. It sits at an angle to the conscious desire rather than agreeing with it: the conscious desire is the reason they give themselves, and this is what keeps them going when that reason runs out. One sentence, third person, by name.

recognized_need.description: Something they know they must do whether they want to or not, and may resent. A real obligation this world imposes on them -- their work, their family, their debt, their oath, their body -- and one that can get in the way of the conscious desire. One sentence, third person, by name.

unrecognized_need.description: What they need and cannot see, not even unconsciously. A reader should be able to see it from the backstory above while they cannot. If they never do it, pursuing the conscious desire ruins them. It must not be the conscious desire said twice. One sentence, third person, by name.

desire_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the CONSCIOUS DESIRE has -- the one that fits the act they would take tomorrow morning.

need_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the UNRECOGNIZED NEED has. It may be the same label as the one above; the more interesting answer is usually a different one.

physics: Gravity is consistent at 9.8 m/s², but the world is veined with ley lines—thin, invisible rivers of latent magic that pulse at a frequency of 0.3 Hz, detectable only by iron-forged compasses. The ley lines are finite; overuse in a region causes them to fade for a century. No magic can resurrect the dead or heal mortal wounds, only delay them.
technology: The world is locked in a late medieval stasis, with iron and steel as the primary metals. Clockwork mechanisms exist but are rare, limited to devices no larger than a loaf of bread due to the scarcity of precision gears. Gunpowder is known but unstable, often exploding prematurely in 1 out of 5 attempts. Most advancements are suppressed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre, which burns any invention deemed heretical.
geographies: The kingdom of Durnhold is a land of jagged iron cliffs and black pine forests, its heart dominated by the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano where the Church burns heretics. The goblin caves lie beneath the Spire’s roots, a labyrinth of obsidian tunnels lit by bioluminescent fungi that dim every 12 hours. The nearest town, Hollow’s End, is a day’s ride north, its walls built from the bones of ancient trolls. The river Veyth, wide and slow, marks the border between Durnhold and the goblin territories, its waters undrinkable due to high iron content.
races: Durnish, Goblins, Trollkin, Veythi
civilizations: The Kingdom of Durnhold is ruled by the Iron Council, a cabal of knights and priests who enforce the Church’s decrees from the Obsidian Throne in the capital, Spire’s Rest. The goblins are divided into warring clans, the largest being the Blackfang, who control the dungeon where the prince is held. The Trollkin have no settlements, only nomadic bands, while the Veythi operate from floating barges on the river, their only permanent structure being the Rust Market, a black-market hub hidden in the river’s mist. The uneasy peace is maintained by the Iron Council’s threat of annihilation and the goblins’ fear of open war, but raids and executions are common.

title: The Iron Gate Descends
genre: dark fantasy
preface: The iron gate groans as it settles into the stone, its teeth biting into the threshold with a finality that echoes through the cavern. You stand in the dim glow of bioluminescent fungi, the air thick with the scent of damp earth and old blood. Your gauntleted hand rests on the hilt of your Veldarian sword, its edge still sharp despite the weight of the blackened plate armor pressing into your shoulders. The prince’s signet ring, cold in your palm, was found in the mud outside this gate—proof he passed this way. Behind you, the tunnel slopes upward, but the way forward is a yawning maw of obsidian, the walls slick with moisture. Somewhere in the dark, something skitters.

The prince’s signet ring, discovered in the mud, confirms his passage into the tunnels. The air is thick with the scent of damp earth and the faint glow of fungi, while the distant sound of movement hints at unseen dangers ahead. The Church’s decree to retrieve the prince or die trying weighs heavily, but the immediate threat is the darkness itself.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

One sentence, third person, by name.

A narrow path winds upward, marked by the charred remains of old watchfires, their embers long cold. The Spire looms above, its jagged peak wreathed in smoke that stains the sky a dull, sooty orange.
detail.lore: This slope is the outer skin of the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano repurposed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre as its seat of execution. The ground here is rich with iron ore, which the Church mines to fuel its forges and pyres, leaving the earth scarred and brittle. The cave mouth behind you is one of many entrances to the goblin tunnels, long ignored by the Iron Council until the prince’s disappearance forced their hand. The wind carries the stench of the pyres, a constant reminder of the Church’s power and the cost of heresy.

items.name: iron shard

people.personality: Harkin speaks in a low, gravelly voice, his words measured but sharp with the weight of years. He treats strangers with cautious respect, though his eyes flicker with the wariness of someone who has spent a lifetime on the wrong side of the law.
people.backstory: Harkin Veyth was once a smuggler for the Rust Market, ferrying contraband along the Veyth under the cover of its iron-tainted mists. Age has slowed his hands, but not his mind, and he now trades in information rather than goods, selling secrets to those who can afford them. He came to the Spire’s slopes today to meet a contact, but the Church’s pyres have driven the man away.
people.likes: whiskey, old stories, quiet bargains
people.dislikes: the Church, loud noises, wasted time
people.conscious_desire: Harkin wants to sell the location of a hidden cache of clockwork gears to the highest bidder.
people.unconscious_desire: Harkin wants to prove he is still useful, even as his body betrays him.
people.recognized_need: Harkin must avoid the Iron Council’s notice, or his knowledge will be burned along with his body.
people.unrecognized_need: Harkin needs to pass his trade to someone younger before his luck runs out.

title: The Iron Gate Descends

## Universe Details
physics: Gravity is consistent at 9.8 m/s², but the world is veined with ley lines—thin, invisible rivers of latent magic that pulse at a frequency of 0.3 Hz, detectable only by iron-forged compasses. These lines can be tapped by blood rituals, but each use drains the caster’s lifespan by exactly one day per minute of magic. The ley lines are finite; overuse in a region causes them to fade for a century. No magic can resurrect the dead or heal mortal wounds, only delay them.
technology: The world is locked in a late medieval stasis, with iron and steel as the primary metals. Clockwork mechanisms exist but are rare, limited to devices no larger than a loaf of bread due to the scarcity of precision gears. Gunpowder is known but unstable, often exploding prematurely in 1 out of 5 attempts. Most advancements are suppressed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre, which burns any invention deemed heretical.
geographies: The kingdom of Durnhold is a land of jagged iron cliffs and black pine forests, its heart dominated by the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano where the Church burns heretics. The goblin caves lie beneath the Spire’s roots, a labyrinth of obsidian tunnels lit by bioluminescent fungi that dim every 12 hours. The nearest town, Hollow’s End, is a day’s ride north, its walls built from the bones of ancient trolls. The river Veyth, wide and slow, marks the border between Durnhold and the goblin territories, its waters undrinkable due to high iron content.
races: Durnish, Goblins, Trollkin, Veythi
civilizations: The Kingdom of Durnhold is ruled by the Iron Council, a cabal of knights and priests who enforce the Church’s decrees from the Obsidian Throne in the capital, Spire’s Rest. The goblins are divided into warring clans, the largest being the Blackfang, who control the dungeon where the prince is held. The Trollkin have no settlements, only nomadic bands, while the Veythi operate from floating barges on the river, their only permanent structure being the Rust Market, a black-market hub hidden in the river’s mist. The uneasy peace is maintained by the Iron Council’s threat of annihilation and the goblins’ fear of open war, but raids and executions are common.


## Story Details
title: The Iron Gate Descends
genre: dark fantasy
preface: The iron gate groans as it settles into the stone, its teeth biting into the threshold with a finality that echoes through the cavern. You stand in the dim glow of bioluminescent fungi, the air thick with the scent of damp earth and old blood. Your gauntleted hand rests on the hilt of your Veldarian sword, its edge still sharp despite the weight of the blackened plate armor pressing into your shoulders. The prince’s signet ring, cold in your palm, was found in the mud outside this gate—proof he passed this way. Behind you, the tunnel slopes upward, but the way forward is a yawning maw of obsidian, the walls slick with moisture. Somewhere in the dark, something skitters.

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: The 2 people who are in this place right now. Write all 2 the instructions describe, in the order they are given there.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

unconscious_desire.description: What they are actually pursuing and would deny if you said it to them. It sits at an angle to the conscious desire rather than agreeing with it: the conscious desire is the reason they give themselves, and this is what keeps them going when that reason runs out. One sentence, third person, by name.

recognized_need.description: Something they know they must do whether they want to or not, and may resent. A real obligation this world imposes on them -- their work, their family, their debt, their oath, their body -- and one that can get in the way of the conscious desire. One sentence, third person, by name.

unrecognized_need.description: What they need and cannot see, not even unconsciously. A reader should be able to see it from the backstory above while they cannot. If they never do it, pursuing the conscious desire ruins them. It must not be the conscious desire said twice. One sentence, third person, by name.

desire_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the CONSCIOUS DESIRE has -- the one that fits the act they would take tomorrow morning.

need_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the UNRECOGNIZED NEED has. It may be the same label as the one above; the more interesting answer is usually a different one.

people.appearance: A wiry goblin with patchy green skin and a mop of greasy black hair tied back with a strip of leather. Their eyes dart nervously, and their fingers tap restlessly against the hilt of a chipped dagger at their belt.
people.personality: Rik is quick to laugh but quicker to flee, their humor masking a deep-seated paranoia. They treat strangers with cautious curiosity, always weighing the risk of betrayal against the potential for gain.

people.likes: sharp blades, dark corners, stolen trinkets
people.dislikes: Church knights, bright lights, loud noises
people.conscious_desire: Rik wants to slip past the city gates and return to the goblin caves with news of the Council’s plans.
people.unconscious_desire: Rik wants to prove they’re more than just a lowly scout, that they deserve a place at the Blackfang war table.
people.recognized_need: Rik must avoid the Church’s patrols, or they’ll be burned alive for heresy.
people.unrecognized_need: Rik needs to trust someone, but they’ve never learned how.

people.appearance: A hulking trollkin with graying, matted fur and a face lined with old scars. His massive frame is hunched slightly, as if bracing against an unseen weight, and his hands are wrapped in thick leather to hide the burns from his past.
people.personality: Gorruk speaks in a low, rumbling voice, his words deliberate and heavy with the weight of years. He is slow to anger but impossible to sway once his mind is made up, and he treats strangers with a gruff but not unkind demeanor.
people.backstory: Gorruk Stonehide was once a smith for the Iron Council, forging the weapons that fueled the Church’s purges. But after witnessing the execution of a child accused of heresy, he fled, only to be captured and branded a traitor. Now, he wanders the edges of Durnhold, selling his skills to those who need them, though he knows the Council will never stop hunting him.
people.likes: quiet forges, honest work, the smell of hot metal
people.conscious_desire: Gorruk wants to find a safe place to rebuild his life, far from the Church’s reach.
people.unconscious_desire: Gorruk wants to atone for the lives his hammers took, though he’ll never admit it.
people.recognized_need: Gorruk must keep moving, or the Iron Council’s hunters will find him.
people.unrecognized_need: Gorruk needs to let go of the guilt that chains him to the past.

You stand in the dim glow of bioluminescent fungi, the air thick with the scent of damp earth and old blood. Your gauntleted hand rests on the hilt of your Veldarian sword, its edge still sharp despite the weight of the blackened plate armor pressing into your shoulders. The prince’s signet ring, cold in your palm, was found in the mud outside this gate—proof he passed this way. Behind you, the tunnel slopes upward, but the way forward is a yawning maw of obsidian, the walls slick with moisture. Somewhere in the dark, something skitters.

The prince’s signet ring, discovered in the mud, confirms his passage into the tunnels. The air is thick with the scent of damp earth and the faint glow of fungi, while the distant sound of movement hints at unseen dangers ahead. The Church’s decree to retrieve the prince or die trying weighs heavily, but the immediate threat is the darkness itself.

detail.lore: The Blackfang Warren is a labyrinth of tunnels and chambers beneath the Ashen Spire, hewn by the Blackfang clan to store their spoils and prisoners. The fungi that light the warren pulse faintly in time with the ley lines, though their glow dims every half-day, plunging sections into darkness. This is where the Blackfang keep what they take—and what they fear.

## Universe Details
physics: Gravity is consistent at 9.8 m/s², but the world is veined with ley lines—thin, invisible rivers of latent magic that pulse at a frequency of 0.3 Hz, detectable only by iron-forged compasses. These lines can be tapped by blood rituals, but each use drains the caster’s lifespan by exactly one day per minute of magic. The ley lines are finite; overuse in a region causes them to fade for a century. No magic can resurrect the dead or heal mortal wounds, only delay them.
technology: The world is locked in a late medieval stasis, with iron and steel as the primary metals. Clockwork mechanisms exist but are rare, limited to devices no larger than a loaf of bread due to the scarcity of precision gears. Gunpowder is known but unstable, often exploding prematurely in 1 out of 5 attempts. Most advancements are suppressed by the Church of the Eternal Pyre, which burns any invention deemed heretical.
geographies: The kingdom of Durnhold is a land of jagged iron cliffs and black pine forests, its heart dominated by the Ashen Spire, a dead volcano where the Church burns heretics. The goblin caves lie beneath the Spire’s roots, a labyrinth of obsidian tunnels lit by bioluminescent fungi that dim every 12 hours. The nearest town, Hollow’s End, is a day’s ride north, its walls built from the bones of ancient trolls. The river Veyth, wide and slow, marks the border between Durnhold and the goblin territories, its waters undrinkable due to high iron content.
races: Durnish, Goblins, Trollkin, Veythi
civilizations: The Kingdom of Durnhold is ruled by the Iron Council, a cabal of knights and priests who enforce the Church’s decrees from the Obsidian Throne in the capital, Spire’s Rest. The goblins are divided into warring clans, the largest being the Blackfang, who control the dungeon where the prince is held. The Trollkin have no settlements, only nomadic bands, while the Veythi operate from floating barges on the river, their only permanent structure being the Rust Market, a black-market hub hidden in the river’s mist. The uneasy peace is maintained by the Iron Council’s threat of annihilation and the goblins’ fear of open war, but raids and executions are common.

detail.description: You stand in a dim, wood-paneled room where the scent of salt and old paper lingers. A heavy oak desk dominates the space, its surface cluttered with ledgers and ink-stained parchment. A single oil lamp flickers on a side table, casting long shadows across the floorboards. The east wall holds a sturdy door, its brass handle tarnished, while a narrow staircase spirals upward in the corner. The air is thick with the quiet hum of the quay outside, muted by the thick stone walls.
detail.lore: This is the main receiving room of the Custom House, where incoming goods were once logged and duties collected. Built a century ago, its walls have absorbed the comings and goings of countless ships and merchants. The desk has stood here since the beginning, its drawers filled with records of every cargo that passed through the port. The lamp was lit this morning, though no one admits to having been here since noon.

items.name: an oil lamp
items.description: A brass lamp with a glass chimney, half-filled with oil. The wick is trimmed but unlit.

people.personality: Mara is sharp-eyed and direct, with a dry wit that cuts through small talk. She treats strangers with cautious curiosity, sizing them up before deciding whether to engage.
people.backstory: Mara grew up on the docks, learning the trade of a customs clerk from her father. She took over his post after he retired, but her meticulous nature often puts her at odds with the more relaxed harbourfolk. She was the last to leave the Custom House at noon, locking the door behind her.
people.likes: order, ledgers, quiet mornings
people.fears: being accused of negligence, the tide taking something irreplaceable
people.conscious_desire: Mara wants to prove the Custom House was properly secured at noon.
people.unconscious_desire: Mara wants to uncover the truth behind the broken seal, even if it implicates someone she respects.
people.recognized_need: Mara must maintain the integrity of the customs records, no matter the cost.
people.unrecognized_need: Mara needs to trust that others can share the responsibility of keeping the port honest.

people.appearance: A stout Harbourfolk woman with silver-streaked hair pulled into a tight bun. Her face is lined with years of squinting into the sun, and her hands are calloused from decades of handling ropes and cargo.
people.personality: Tessa is gruff but not unkind, with a voice that carries the weight of experience. She speaks in short, blunt sentences and has little patience for nonsense.
people.backstory: Tessa has worked the docks since she was a girl, first as a stevedore and later as a forewoman overseeing the unloading of ships. She retired years ago but still visits the Custom House out of habit, keeping an eye on the younger folk. She noticed the broken seal first and came inside to investigate.
people.likes: hard work, a well-tied knot, a fair day's wage
people.dislikes: laziness, broken promises, storms at sea
people.fears: the port falling into disrepair, being forgotten
people.conscious_desire: Tessa wants to find out who broke the seal and why.
people.unconscious_desire: Tessa wants to ensure the Custom House remains a place of trust, even if it means confronting old friends.
people.recognized_need: Tessa must pass on her knowledge to the next generation before she is too old to do so.
people.unrecognized_need: Tessa needs to accept that the port can change without losing its soul.

physics: Ordinary physics, and a tide that keeps to its table.
technology: Rope, tar, lamp oil and a ledger.
geographies: One quay, one custom house standing on it, and the water at the end of both.
races: Harbourfolk
civilizations: A port that has never been anything else.


## Story Details
title: The Quay House
genre: harbour mystery
preface: The custom house has been locked since noon and the seal on the door is broken.
summary: Somebody was inside the custom house when the whole quay says it was empty.


## The Place
name: The Custom House room 3
teaser: A room inside The Custom House, 7 by 6 paces on storey 0.
## Where This Room Is
The game's own records of this room, already decided and not yours to
change. Write the room around them: do not contradict a measurement, and
do not give it a way out this list does not have.
This room is 7 by 6 paces -- about 11 by 9 metres. It is on storey 0 of The Custom House, which is 14 by 10 paces across; storey 0 is the ground floor. Its ways out: a door in the north wall, to The Custom House room 2; a door in the west wall, to The Custom House room 4. Those are every way out of this room, and no other wall of it holds a door.
## Instructions
Write this place out in full.
- The description is what the player reads on arrival. Address them as "you"
- Describe what is here now, not the history -- the history is the lore
- Stay consistent with the universe and with the teaser above
- Respect the stated length of each field
- NAME THIS ROOM. It is one room inside The Custom House. The player reads the room and
  the place together -- "the <your name> of The Custom House" -- so name the ROOM only,
  and never put the place's own name into it. A short noun phrase carrying the
  article English wants on it, 2 to 4 words: "the counting room", "the cold
  store", "the harbourmaster's office". Name it for what the floor plan above
  says this room is and for what you have just described standing in it. Never
  a comma in it

## What Is Lying Here
List AT MOST 3 portable things a player could pick up and carry away.
- Nothing is the right answer for most rooms. An empty list is a complete answer
- Only loose, portable things. Not the door, not the floor, not the machinery
  bolted to it -- something a person could put in a pocket or under an arm
- Each one must be consistent with the description you just wrote, and worth
  the player noticing
- Pick its use_kind from the supplied physical profiles. Ordinary is the
  default. Food and drink can be consumed without healing; healing is only
  a restorative dose this world permits. Firestarters burn combustible
  objects, levers pry jammed passages, lockpicks try locks, and a key only
  opens a passage explicitly matched to it. Mark combustible only when an
  ordinary firestarter can destroy the object. The engine owns the effects
  and their amounts; its description cannot grant extra powers
- If a thing has WRITING on it -- a note, a letter, a handbill, a label, a
  docket, a page, a sign -- mark it readable and WRITE OUT WHAT IS WRITTEN
  ON IT, exactly as it appears on the thing. The words themselves, not a
  description of them, and short enough to finish -- a few words, a line,
  or a few short lines. The game keeps those words and a player reading it
  twice reads the same ones
- Never name it after a person or after a place. Already spoken for in this story, so do not reuse: Nell Cawsand, seal ledger

## Who Is Here
Write EXACTLY 2 people who are in this place right now.
- Anyone you write is somebody the player can walk up to and talk to, so they
  have to have a reason to be standing here and something they want
- Do not write the player, and do not write somebody passing through
- Never give them the name of a place, of a thing, or any name already
  spoken for above

Who they are is already decided. Write these people and do not change them:
  the 1st is Harbourfolk, about 25, male
  the 2nd is Harbourfolk, about 75, female

## Their Four Objects of Desire

Write four things this person is after and pick two labels for them. Work from
everything above -- their backstory, what they like and dislike, what they are
afraid of, how old they are, how strong their will is, and where they are
standing.

The two labels are picked from this list and nothing else:

  keep     They are holding on to something they already have.
  obtain   They are trying to get hold of something they do not have.
  reach    They are trying to get to a particular place.
  attend   They are trying to stay near a particular person.
  avoid    They are trying to get away from a person or a place.
  withhold They are trying to stop somebody else getting something.
  offer    They are trying to put something into somebody else's hands.

Rules:
- Every one of the four names something to move TOWARD. A field that only says
  what they want to stop or escape is not finished. Say what is on the other
  side of it.
- Write them so an ordinary act in a room could serve one: picking something
  up, handing something over, walking out, staying put, standing near
  somebody. Do not write a desire nobody could act on in a room.
- Keep them consistent with the fears and dislikes above. A fear is usually the
  shadow of one of these four and should read that way.
- The conscious desire and the unrecognized need must not be the same thing
  said twice.
- Write in the third person, by name.
- Do not resolve any of them, and do not say how the story ends.
- Respect the stated length of each field.
- Each person in this room gets their own four. Two people in one room must not
  want the same thing in the same words.
- At least one of them should want something that is in this room or one step
  out of it.

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: The 2 people who are in this place right now. Write all 2 the instructions describe, in the order they are given there.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

unconscious_desire.description: What they are actually pursuing and would deny if you said it to them. It sits at an angle to the conscious desire rather than agreeing with it: the conscious desire is the reason they give themselves, and this is what keeps them going when that reason runs out. One sentence, third person, by name.

recognized_need.description: Something they know they must do whether they want to or not, and may resent. A real obligation this world imposes on them -- their work, their family, their debt, their oath, their body -- and one that can get in the way of the conscious desire. One sentence, third person, by name.

unrecognized_need.description: What they need and cannot see, not even unconsciously. A reader should be able to see it from the backstory above while they cannot. If they never do it, pursuing the conscious desire ruins them. It must not be the conscious desire said twice. One sentence, third person, by name.

desire_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the CONSCIOUS DESIRE has -- the one that fits the act they would take tomorrow morning.

need_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the UNRECOGNIZED NEED has. It may be the same label as the one above; the more interesting answer is usually a different one.

detail.description: You stand in a dim, windowless chamber where the air carries the sharp tang of ink and old paper. A single oil lamp flickers on a scarred wooden desk, casting long shadows over stacks of ledgers and a broken wax seal lying near the door. The stone walls are bare except for a faded tally chart pinned to the north wall, its edges yellowed with age. The floorboards creak faintly underfoot, worn smooth by decades of hurried footsteps.
detail.lore: This was once the ledger room of the custom house, where harbourfolk recorded the comings and goings of every ship and cargo. The broken seal suggests someone forced their way in recently, though the ledgers themselves appear untouched. The tally chart tracks the tide tables, a relic of a time when the port’s rhythms were simpler. The desk has stood here since the building’s first days, its surface etched with the names of long-dead clerks.
detail.name: the ledger room

items.name: broken wax seal
items.description: A shattered red wax seal, its fragments scattered near the door. The impression is too damaged to read, but the wax is still soft in places.

items.name: tally chart
items.description: A large, yellowed sheet of paper pinned to the wall, covered in handwritten tide tables and faded ink notations.
items.inscription: Tide Table: High at 6, Low at 12. Spring tides marked in red.

people.appearance: A lean Harbourfolk man of about 25, his dark hair tied back in a loose knot. He wears a patched but clean tunic, the sleeves rolled up to his elbows, and his hands are ink-stained from long hours at the ledger.
people.personality: Quiet and methodical, Tobias speaks in measured tones, though his eyes dart nervously to the broken seal every few moments. He treats strangers with cautious politeness, as if unsure whether they’re friend or foe.
people.backstory: Tobias was the junior clerk assigned to this room, tasked with maintaining the ledgers and tide records. He arrived this morning to find the door unsealed and has been searching for answers ever since. He suspects someone tampered with the records but can’t bring himself to admit it.
people.likes: order, quiet, precise handwriting
people.conscious_desire: Tobias wants to find out who broke the seal and restore the room to its proper state.
people.unconscious_desire: Tobias wants to prove he is more than just a clerk, that he can uncover the truth others overlook.
people.recognized_need: Tobias must report the broken seal to the harbourmaster, whether he wants to or not.
people.unrecognized_need: Tobias needs to trust someone else with the truth, even if it risks his own standing.

people.appearance: A stout Harbourfolk woman in her mid-70s, her silver hair braided tightly and her face lined with years of squinting at ledgers. She leans on a gnarled walking stick, her sharp eyes missing nothing.
people.personality: Mara is blunt and no-nonsense, speaking her mind without hesitation. She has little patience for hesitation or secrecy, though she softens slightly when she sees someone genuinely trying.
people.backstory: Mara was the senior clerk here for decades before retiring, and she still visits the custom house out of habit. She arrived today to check on the ledgers and found Tobias in a state of distress. She knows the room’s secrets better than anyone and is determined to protect its integrity.
people.likes: honesty, tradition, strong tea
people.fears: losing control, the past repeating itself
people.conscious_desire: Mara wants to ensure the ledgers remain accurate and untampered with.
people.unconscious_desire: Mara wants to prove she is still needed, that her knowledge and experience cannot be replaced.
people.recognized_need: Mara must train Tobias to take over her old duties, whether she likes it or not.
people.unrecognized_need: Mara needs to let go of the past and trust the next generation to carry on without her.

requests.system:
You build the rooms of a text adventure one at a time. You write places a
player can stand in and walk out of: concrete, specific, and consistent
with the world they belong to. Every exit you name is somewhere the player
could actually go.

DO NOT INCLUDE EMOJIS IN YOUR RESPONSE.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true.
