appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

The east wall holds a sturdy door, its brass handle tarnished, while a narrow staircase spirals upward in the west corner. A heavy, bolted door to the south opens onto the quay, letting in the faint sound of lapping water and the cry of gulls.
detail.lore: This is the main receiving room of the custom house, where incoming goods were once logged before being moved to the records room. Built a century ago from ship timber, it has seen generations of harbourfolk pass through its doors. The desk was once manned by clerks who tallied every barrel and bale, but now it stands empty, a silent witness to the mystery of the broken seal.

people.personality: He speaks with the slow, measured cadence of someone used to being obeyed, but there’s a restlessness in his eyes, as if he’s waiting for something to go wrong. He treats strangers with polite suspicion, his questions direct and his answers sparse.
people.backstory: Tobias Veyne was once the senior clerk of the custom house, overseeing the ledgers and the men who kept them. He retired five years ago but still visits the building out of habit, or perhaps guilt. He was the last to lock the door the night before the seal was broken, and the mystery of who was inside gnaws at him.

people.dislikes: dishonesty, wasted time, the taste of cheap rum
people.fears: being blamed for something he did not do, the sea at night
people.conscious_desire: Tobias wants to prove that the custom house was properly secured the night before the seal was broken.
people.unconscious_desire: Tobias wants to uncover the truth behind the broken seal, even if it implicates someone he once trusted.
people.recognized_need: Tobias must maintain the reputation of the custom house, as its former overseer.
people.unrecognized_need: Tobias needs to accept that his time in charge is over and that the new generation must take responsibility for their own mistakes.

detail.description: You stand in a dim, wood-paneled entry hall where the scent of salt and old ledgers lingers in the air. A single oil lamp flickers on a wall sconce, casting long shadows across the scuffed plank floor. The western exit opens onto the quay, where the sound of lapping water and distant gulls drifts in.
detail.lore: This is the ground-floor entry of the custom house, built a century ago to oversee the port’s duties and tariffs. Harbourfolk have passed through here daily for generations, though today its usual bustle is absent. The broken seal on the east door suggests someone entered after hours, leaving no record of their visit.

items.name: a lantern
items.description: A brass lantern with a cracked glass pane, its wick dry and its oil long since spent. It sits on the floor near the stair.

people.appearance: A broad-shouldered harbourfolk with silver-streaked hair tied back in a neat queue. His face is weathered by decades of salt air, and his hands, though steady, bear the callouses of a man who has worked ropes and ledgers alike.
people.personality: He speaks slowly, as if weighing each word, and his gaze lingers on the broken seal with a mix of frustration and resignation. He treats strangers with cautious politeness, but his patience is thin today.
people.backstory: Tobias Harkin has been the custom house clerk for thirty years, a post he inherited from his father. He arrived this morning to find the door unsealed and the ledger out of place, a breach of protocol that gnaws at him. He wants to know who was here and why, but the answers elude him.
people.likes: order, quiet mornings, the smell of fresh ink
people.dislikes: dishonesty, broken routines, the taste of cheap rum
people.fears: being blamed for the breach, the tide taking his records
people.conscious_desire: Tobias wants to restore the ledger to its proper place and re-seal the door before the harbourmaster arrives.
people.unconscious_desire: Tobias wants to uncover the truth behind the broken seal, even if it means admitting his own oversight.
people.recognized_need: Tobias must account for every duty collected, as the harbourmaster demands.
people.unrecognized_need: Tobias needs to accept that some mysteries cannot be solved by ledgers alone.

detail.description: You stand in a dim, wood-paneled room where the scent of lamp oil and old paper lingers thick in the air. A single iron-bound desk sits against the west wall, its surface cluttered with ledgers and a half-empty inkwell. The floorboards creak underfoot, and the faint sound of lapping water seeps through the cracks. A broken wax seal lies near the door, its red imprint smeared across the floor. The east door stands slightly ajar, revealing a sliver of the next room, while a narrow stairway ascends to the upper floor.
detail.lore: This is the main receiving room of the custom house, where incoming goods were once logged and duties assessed. Built by the harbourmaster’s guild a century ago, it has seen generations of clerks come and go, though its purpose has never wavered. The broken seal suggests someone forced entry recently, yet the room itself shows no other signs of struggle. The desk and ledgers remain untouched, as if the intruder sought something beyond mere records.

people.backstory: Mara Vey has been the custom house’s head clerk for forty years, long enough to remember when the harbourmaster’s son still played in the streets. She was the last to lock the door at noon, and now she stands here, bewildered, because the seal she set herself is broken. people.recognized_need: Mara must account for every ledger and page before the harbourmaster returns at dusk.
people.unrecognized_need: Mara needs to admit that her eyes are no longer sharp enough to catch every discrepancy.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

people.backstory: Mira Vey was once a clerk in Ward 7 before her records were lost in a fire that the Registry never fully documented. She now trades in salvaged paper and forgotten seals, moving through the wards with a quiet defiance. She is here because she heard the Inspectorate was coming, and she wants to see who they take this time.

people.dislikes: loud voices, locked doors, being watched
people.fears: forgetting her own name, the Sealed Room
people.conscious_desire: Mira wants to slip past the Inspectorate and reach the supply closet before they do.
people.unconscious_desire: Mira wants to find a record with her name on it, even if it is not hers anymore.
people.recognized_need: Mira must avoid drawing the attention of the Inspectorate, whose questions she cannot answer without risking her precarious existence.
people.unrecognized_need: Mira needs to accept that some doors will never open for her again, no matter how hard she tries.

people.appearance: A woman of middle height, her dark hair pulled into a severe bun, her coat buttoned to the throat. Her boots are polished to a mirror shine, and her fingers tap restlessly against her thigh.
people.personality: She is brisk and efficient, her voice clipped and her manner no-nonsense. She does not suffer fools but will tolerate incompetence if it does not slow her down.

people.likes: order, punctuality, well-kept ledgers
people.conscious_desire: Elspeth wants to collect the supply closet’s inventory log before the hour is out.
people.unconscious_desire: Elspeth wants to prove that she is the one who sees what others miss, even if it means digging into places she is not supposed to go.
people.recognized_need: Elspeth must attend to the details of every door and desk, because the Registry demands nothing less.
people.unrecognized_need: Elspeth needs to admit that some gaps in the records are there for a reason, and that filling them might unravel more than she can control.

people.personality: She is soft-spoken but relentless, her questions gentle but persistent. She has a habit of humming old tunes under her breath, as if to fill the silence.
people.backstory: Tansy Rook was once a Marginalia scribe before her hands gave out, and now she drifts through the wards, collecting stories the Registry would rather forget. people.dislikes: cold drafts, locked drawers, being ignored
people.conscious_desire: Tansy wants to find the door that used to be where the supply closet is now.

prompts.detail:
## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws hold, with one exception: in the city of Ambry and the wards around it, a thing that is not written down stops being reliably itself. The effect is slow and dull rather than dramatic. An unrecorded corridor will, over a season, start to run a few feet short. An unregistered tool loses its temper and its edge. A person whose file is closed is not struck down; they are simply harder to remember, then harder to see, then gone from the accounts of everyone who knew them, until the only evidence they existed is what somebody wrote. Nothing about this is reversible by force. It is reversible by paperwork, which is why the Registry rules here.
technology: Roughly late nineteenth century, and skewed hard toward anything that copies or preserves. Ambry has pneumatic tube post between every ward office, carbon paper, wax cylinders, a functioning telegraph and no electricity in the residential wards. Presses, seals, indelible inks and lamp-lit copy rooms are the industry the city actually runs on. There are no engines to speak of outside the pumping stations, because an engine that is not maintained on a filed schedule stops working in ways engineers find distressing rather than interesting.
geographies: Ambry sits in a wide river delta that floods twice a year. The Registry occupies the whole of the high ground: eleven storeys of ward offices, copy rooms and stacks, built in rings around a courtyard nobody has permission to cross. Below it the Middle Wards spread out in numbered blocks, each one a warren of tenements and copying shops. Beyond the levee are the flood plains, unsurveyed and therefore unrecorded, where the Unwritten live in houses that move with the water. The Registry's own basements run four floors below the flood line and are dry, which nobody has ever satisfactorily explained.
races: Copyists' Line, Ledger-Kept, Marginalia, Unwritten
civilizations: One city, one institution, and a functional caste order underneath it. The Registry employs one adult in six and files the rest. Above the clerks sit the Inspectorate, who audit; above them the Sealed Room, which nobody in this story has seen. Below everyone are the Marginalia, whose records were damaged or amended and who consequently take the work that ought not be remembered. Out past the levee the Unwritten trade fish, salt and salvage into a city that will not put their names on a receipt. Everyone in Ambry is polite, and everyone counts the days since their file was last touched.


## Story Details
title: The Unrecorded Hour
genre: bureaucratic mystery
preface: The stamp is still in your hand and the ink is still wet, and there is an hour missing out of the middle of your own daybook. Not a blank line: a clean, ruled gap between four and five o'clock, in your handwriting, with the running total carried straight across it as though nothing needed to be entered at all. You have worked Ward Office 12 for eleven years and you have never carried a total across a gap in your life. Rain is coming off the levee and going sideways past the window. Somewhere down the long hallway a door closes, and then another, nearer -- the Inspectorate does its rounds at seven and it is twenty past six. Perrin's desk across the room has been cleared to the wood, and you cannot remember when, or by whom, or -- and this is the part that has your hands cold -- whether there was ever anybody sitting at it. There is one thing in this office nobody has audited in eleven years, and its door is behind you.
summary: The player is a ward clerk in Ambry who finds an hour cut out of their own daybook and the desk opposite theirs cleared of a colleague they can no longer quite remember. Working out what happened in that hour means going through the Registry's own paperwork against it: the supply closet nobody has inventoried, the long hallway with the Inspectorate coming up it, and eventually the question of who has blank writs and why one was spent on a Marginalia clerk in Ward Office 12. The tone is dry, close and procedural, and the horror is entirely administrative.

teaser: Doors closing one after another, and shoes you can already hear.

- The description is what the player reads on arrival. Address them as "you"

Write EXACTLY 3 people who are in this place right now.

  have to have a reason to be standing here and something they want

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: The 3 people who are in this place right now. Write all 3 the instructions describe, in the order they are given there.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

unconscious_desire.description: What they are actually pursuing and would deny if you said it to them. It sits at an angle to the conscious desire rather than agreeing with it: the conscious desire is the reason they give themselves, and this is what keeps them going when that reason runs out. One sentence, third person, by name.

recognized_need.description: Something they know they must do whether they want to or not, and may resent. A real obligation this world imposes on them -- their work, their family, their debt, their oath, their body -- and one that can get in the way of the conscious desire. One sentence, third person, by name.

unrecognized_need.description: What they need and cannot see, not even unconsciously. A reader should be able to see it from the backstory above while they cannot. If they never do it, pursuing the conscious desire ruins them. It must not be the conscious desire said twice. One sentence, third person, by name.

desire_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the CONSCIOUS DESIRE has -- the one that fits the act they would take tomorrow morning.

need_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the UNRECOGNIZED NEED has. It may be the same label as the one above; the more interesting answer is usually a different one.

history.content:
## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws hold, with one exception: in the city of Ambry and the wards around it, a thing that is not written down stops being reliably itself. The effect is slow and dull rather than dramatic. An unrecorded corridor will, over a season, start to run a few feet short. An unregistered tool loses its temper and its edge. A person whose file is closed is not struck down; they are simply harder to remember, then harder to see, then gone from the accounts of everyone who knew them, until the only evidence they existed is what somebody wrote. Nothing about this is reversible by force. It is reversible by paperwork, which is why the Registry rules here.
technology: Roughly late nineteenth century, and skewed hard toward anything that copies or preserves. Ambry has pneumatic tube post between every ward office, carbon paper, wax cylinders, a functioning telegraph and no electricity in the residential wards. Presses, seals, indelible inks and lamp-lit copy rooms are the industry the city actually runs on. There are no engines to speak of outside the pumping stations, because an engine that is not maintained on a filed schedule stops working in ways engineers find distressing rather than interesting.
geographies: Ambry sits in a wide river delta that floods twice a year. The Registry occupies the whole of the high ground: eleven storeys of ward offices, copy rooms and stacks, built in rings around a courtyard nobody has permission to cross. Below it the Middle Wards spread out in numbered blocks, each one a warren of tenements and copying shops. Beyond the levee are the flood plains, unsurveyed and therefore unrecorded, where the Unwritten live in houses that move with the water. The Registry's own basements run four floors below the flood line and are dry, which nobody has ever satisfactorily explained.
races: Copyists' Line, Ledger-Kept, Marginalia, Unwritten
civilizations: One city, one institution, and a functional caste order underneath it. The Registry employs one adult in six and files the rest. Above the clerks sit the Inspectorate, who audit; above them the Sealed Room, which nobody in this story has seen. Below everyone are the Marginalia, whose records were damaged or amended and who consequently take the work that ought not be remembered. Out past the levee the Unwritten trade fish, salt and salvage into a city that will not put their names on a receipt. Everyone in Ambry is polite, and everyone counts the days since their file was last touched.


## Story Details
title: The Unrecorded Hour
genre: bureaucratic mystery
preface: The stamp is still in your hand and the ink is still wet, and there is an hour missing out of the middle of your own daybook. Not a blank line: a clean, ruled gap between four and five o'clock, in your handwriting, with the running total carried straight across it as though nothing needed to be entered at all. You have worked Ward Office 12 for eleven years and you have never carried a total across a gap in your life. Rain is coming off the levee and going sideways past the window. Somewhere down the long hallway a door closes, and then another, nearer -- the Inspectorate does its rounds at seven and it is twenty past six. Perrin's desk across the room has been cleared to the wood, and you cannot remember when, or by whom, or -- and this is the part that has your hands cold -- whether there was ever anybody sitting at it. There is one thing in this office nobody has audited in eleven years, and its door is behind you.
summary: The player is a ward clerk in Ambry who finds an hour cut out of their own daybook and the desk opposite theirs cleared of a colleague they can no longer quite remember. Working out what happened in that hour means going through the Registry's own paperwork against it: the supply closet nobody has inventoried, the long hallway with the Inspectorate coming up it, and eventually the question of who has blank writs and why one was spent on a Marginalia clerk in Ward Office 12. The tone is dry, close and procedural, and the horror is entirely administrative.

- Stay consistent with the universe and with the teaser above
- Respect the stated length of each field

  bolted to it -- something a person could put in a pocket or under an arm
- Each one must be consistent with the description you just wrote, and worth
  the player noticing

  default. Food and drink can be consumed without healing; healing is only
  a restorative dose this world permits. Firestarters burn combustible

  opens a passage explicitly matched to it. Mark combustible only when an

  and their amounts; its description cannot grant extra powers

  description of them, and short enough to finish -- a few words, a line,

  twice reads the same ones

## Who Is Here
Write EXACTLY 3 people who are in this place right now.
- Anyone you write is somebody the player can walk up to and talk to, so they
  have to have a reason to be standing here and something they want
- Do not write the player, and do not write somebody passing through

  spoken for above

Who they are is already decided. Write these people and do not change them:
  the 1st is Copyists' Line, about 54, non-binary
  the 2nd is Ledger-Kept, about 24, non-binary
  the 3rd is Ledger-Kept, about 36, non-binary

## Their Four Objects of Desire

Write four things this person is after and pick two labels for them. Work from
everything above -- their backstory, what they like and dislike, what they are
afraid of, how old they are, how strong their will is, and where they are
standing.

The two labels are picked from this list and nothing else:

  obtain   They are trying to get hold of something they do not have.
  reach    They are trying to get to a particular place.
  attend   They are trying to stay near a particular person.
  avoid    They are trying to get away from a person or a place.

  offer    They are trying to put something into somebody else's hands.

  side of it.

  up, handing something over, walking out, staying put, standing near
  somebody. Do not write a desire nobody could act on in a room.
- Keep them consistent with the fears and dislikes above. A fear is usually the

  said twice.

- Respect the stated length of each field.

  out of it.

detail.description: You stand in the belly of the Vestry Hulk, where the air is thick with the scent of salt, tar, and old paper. The hull groans softly as the tide laps against its timbers outside, and the dim light from a single oil lamp casts long shadows across the warped decking. Shelves of weathered wood line the walls, sagging under the weight of ledgers, dockets, and rolled charts, all bound with fraying twine. A low table holds an inkwell, its contents long since dried, and a single chair, its legs uneven on the sloping floor. The sound of water shifting against the hull is constant, a slow, rhythmic reminder of the sea’s patience.
detail.lore: The Vestry Hulk was once the revenue cutter *Vestry*, driven ashore in 1836 during a storm so fierce the crew abandoned her to the rocks. She was never floated off, and over the decades, the Assize court repurposed her as its archive, hauling in the county’s legal papers to dry in her hold. Now she serves as the court’s memory, her timbers holding the records of every oath, verdict, and tide mark the coast has ever known. The Shorefolk treat her with wary respect, while the Justicars see her as a necessary evil, a floating vault of truths they must consult but never fully trust.

people.appearance: Lean and sun-browned, with salt-bleached hair tied back in a loose knot. Their sleeves are rolled to the elbows, revealing arms marked with old scars from handling lines and nets. They stand with the easy balance of someone used to shifting decks.
people.personality: Renn speaks in short, sharp sentences, as if every word is a knot they’re tying off. They have little patience for Justicars but will tolerate them if it gets them what they want.
people.backstory: Renn Tallow is Shorefolk, born to a family of wreckers who taught them to read the water before they could read a book. They came to the Vestry Hulk today to retrieve a docket proving their claim to a cargo of silk salvaged last winter, a claim the Justicars have been slow to honor. They’ve been waiting here for hours, watching the tide creep up the hull.
people.likes: salvage, sharp knives, a fair wind
people.fears: being trapped inland, losing a claim
people.conscious_desire: Renn wants to take the silk docket from the Hulk and carry it to the court before the hearing begins.
people.unconscious_desire: Renn wants to prove that the Shorefolk do not need the Justicars to keep their own records straight.
people.recognized_need: Renn must deliver the docket to the court to secure their family’s claim to the silk.
people.unrecognized_need: Renn needs to admit that the Justicars’ records are the only thing that will save Neb Halloran from the tide.

people.appearance: Tall and spare, his black gown hanging from his shoulders like a second skin. His face is lined with years of squinting into the wind, and his hands, though steady, bear the slight tremor of age. He carries a silver-headed cane, though he does not lean on it.
people.personality: Vane speaks in measured tones, each word deliberate, as if he is already writing the verdict. He treats the Hulk like a temple, though he would never call it that aloud.
people.backstory: Elias Vane has served as a Circuit Justicar for forty years, longer than most men live on this coast. He arrived at the Vestry Hulk this morning to review the case against Neb Halloran, but the discrepancy in the tide-slate has unsettled him. He knows the Bell-Keeper’s hand, and he knows the law depends on it.
people.likes: order, precision, the sound of his own voice
people.fears: a verdict built on a lie, the tide turning too soon
people.conscious_desire: Justicar Elias Vane wants to find the original tide-slate entry and confirm the time of high water before the hearing.
people.unconscious_desire: Justicar Elias Vane wants to believe that the law can still hold, even when the water does not.
people.recognized_need: Justicar Elias Vane must uphold the court’s verdict, whatever the tide says.
people.unrecognized_need: Justicar Elias Vane needs to accept that the court’s power depends on the Bell-Keeper’s word more than his own.

people.appearance: Broad-shouldered and silver-haired, his gown straining slightly at the seams. His face is ruddy from years of exposure, and his eyes, though sharp, hold the weariness of a man who has seen too many tides turn against him. He leans heavily on a carved walking stick.
people.personality: Cole is blunt to the point of rudeness, his patience worn thin by decades of listening to liars and fools. He respects the Hulk as a necessary evil but would rather be anywhere else.
people.backstory: Thaddeus Cole was appointed Justicar the same year the *Vestry* beached, and he has outlasted every Bell-Keeper since. He came to the Hulk today to retrieve the wrecking ledger for Neb Halloran’s case, but the altered tide-slate has made him question everything, including his own memory.
people.likes: whiskey, silence, a well-kept ledger
people.dislikes: Shorefolk, the smell of tar, being wrong
people.fears: the court’s authority crumbling, his own mind failing
people.conscious_desire: Justicar Thaddeus Cole wants to take the wrecking ledger from the Hulk and verify the charges against Neb Halloran.
people.unconscious_desire: Justicar Thaddeus Cole wants to prove that he still knows the difference between truth and a lie.
people.recognized_need: Justicar Thaddeus Cole must deliver a verdict that the county will accept, even if the tide does not.
people.unrecognized_need: Justicar Thaddeus Cole needs to admit that he no longer trusts his own judgment as much as he trusts the Bell-Keeper’s.

prompts.detail:
## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws, with one local exception the courts are built around: on this coast an oath spoken over standing salt water binds, and an oath spoken over dry ground does not. Nobody has explained it and everybody has arranged their life around it. A sworn statement made on the causeway at low water holds a man in place -- he cannot walk away from it, cannot contradict it, and will find his own mouth refusing the lie. The same words spoken inland are only words. The binding lasts exactly as long as the water that heard it stays where it is, which on this coast is about six hours.
technology: Sail, tar, oil lamp and iron. Roughly eighteenth century and skewed entirely toward the sea: block and tackle, chain, dredging gear, tide tables computed by hand and reprinted every spring. There is no telegraph and no engine on the coast. The most advanced instrument in the county is the Assize bell, cast to a pitch that carries over surf, and the second is the tide-slate, a ruled board of black slate on which the day's high water is chalked and which no one is permitted to erase but the Bell-Keeper.
geographies: A drowned coast of mud flats, salt marsh and islands that are only islands twice a day. The Assize causeway runs a mile out from the shore to Gallows Rock and is walkable for about five hours either side of low water. On the rock stand the court, the tide post and the beached hulk of the *Vestry*, a revenue cutter that came ashore ninety years ago and was never floated off. Inland the marsh runs to grazing, and beyond that the county town, which the Assizes visit once and never twice.
races: Bell-Keepers, Circuit Justicars, Marshborn, Shorefolk
civilizations: One county, one court, and a hard division between the people of the shore and the people of the marsh. The shore lives by salvage, oysters and the wrecking trade and considers the law a weather event. The marsh lives by grazing and considers itself the county's conscience. Above both sit the Justicars, appointed for life and travelling in circuit, and beside them the Bell-Keepers -- a guild of one family per coast, who read the water and are the only people whose word can rise a court. Everyone here can tell you how long they have until the water turns.


## Story Details
title: The Salt Assizes
genre: tidal legal mystery
preface: You have rung this court up and down for nineteen years and you have never once been wrong about the water, which is why the chalk on the tide-slate is wrong in somebody else's hand. High water is written as ten minutes past eight. High water is at seven. You wrote seven yourself, last night, on a dry board in a still room, and the figure on the slate now is not yours and is close enough to yours to pass. Out at the post, Neb Halloran has been chained since the ebb for a wrecking nobody on this coast believes he did alone, and his hearing is set for the last hour before the turn -- an hour that, on that chalk, does not exist. The Justicar is already in the court with his gown on. The bell is on its hook. Whoever moved seventy minutes has given the water time to do what the court would have had to sign for.
summary: The player is Coraith Vell, Bell-Keeper of the Assize causeway, who finds the day's high water altered by seventy minutes in a hand that is almost her own. The chained man at the tide post has a hearing in an hour the false chalk has erased, so working out who changed it means reading the court's own papers against the water: the Justicar who needs a verdict, the wreck that serves as the vestry, and the question of who benefits from a drowning the record will call a delay. The tone is cold, procedural and out of doors, and the clock is the sea.


## The Place

teaser: A revenue cutter that came ashore in 1836 and is now where the papers live.

  the player noticing

  default. Food and drink can be consumed without healing; healing is only

  and their amounts; its description cannot grant extra powers

- Never name it after a person or after a place. Already spoken for in this story, so do not reuse: Coraith Vell, Ammon Brace, Neb Halloran, Assize tide-slate

## Who Is Here
Write EXACTLY 3 people who are in this place right now.
- Anyone you write is somebody the player can walk up to and talk to, so they
  have to have a reason to be standing here and something they want

  spoken for above

Who they are is already decided. Write these people and do not change them:
  the 1st is Shorefolk, about 26, non-binary
  the 2nd is Circuit Justicars, about 68, trans man
  the 3rd is Circuit Justicars, about 75, trans man

## Their Four Objects of Desire

Write four things this person is after and pick two labels for them. Work from
everything above -- their backstory, what they like and dislike, what they are
afraid of, how old they are, how strong their will is, and where they are
standing.

The two labels are picked from this list and nothing else:

  keep     They are holding on to something they already have.
  obtain   They are trying to get hold of something they do not have.
  reach    They are trying to get to a particular place.
  attend   They are trying to stay near a particular person.
  avoid    They are trying to get away from a person or a place.
  withhold They are trying to stop somebody else getting something.
  offer    They are trying to put something into somebody else's hands.

Rules:
- Every one of the four names something to move TOWARD. A field that only says
  what they want to stop or escape is not finished. Say what is on the other
  side of it.
- Write them so an ordinary act in a room could serve one: picking something
  up, handing something over, walking out, staying put, standing near
  somebody. Do not write a desire nobody could act on in a room.
- Keep them consistent with the fears and dislikes above. A fear is usually the
  shadow of one of these four and should read that way.
- The conscious desire and the unrecognized need must not be the same thing
  said twice.
- Write in the third person, by name.
- Do not resolve any of them, and do not say how the story ends.
- Respect the stated length of each field.
- Each person in this room gets their own four. Two people in one room must not
  want the same thing in the same words.
- At least one of them should want something that is in this room or one step
  out of it.

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: The 3 people who are in this place right now. Write all 3 the instructions describe, in the order they are given there.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

unconscious_desire.description: What they are actually pursuing and would deny if you said it to them. It sits at an angle to the conscious desire rather than agreeing with it: the conscious desire is the reason they give themselves, and this is what keeps them going when that reason runs out. One sentence, third person, by name.

recognized_need.description: Something they know they must do whether they want to or not, and may resent. A real obligation this world imposes on them -- their work, their family, their debt, their oath, their body -- and one that can get in the way of the conscious desire. One sentence, third person, by name.

unrecognized_need.description: What they need and cannot see, not even unconsciously. A reader should be able to see it from the backstory above while they cannot. If they never do it, pursuing the conscious desire ruins them. It must not be the conscious desire said twice. One sentence, third person, by name.

desire_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the CONSCIOUS DESIRE has -- the one that fits the act they would take tomorrow morning.

need_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the UNRECOGNIZED NEED has. It may be the same label as the one above; the more interesting answer is usually a different one.

history.content:
## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws, with one local exception the courts are built around: on this coast an oath spoken over standing salt water binds, and an oath spoken over dry ground does not. Nobody has explained it and everybody has arranged their life around it. A sworn statement made on the causeway at low water holds a man in place -- he cannot walk away from it, cannot contradict it, and will find his own mouth refusing the lie. The same words spoken inland are only words. The binding lasts exactly as long as the water that heard it stays where it is, which on this coast is about six hours.
technology: Sail, tar, oil lamp and iron. Roughly eighteenth century and skewed entirely toward the sea: block and tackle, chain, dredging gear, tide tables computed by hand and reprinted every spring. There is no telegraph and no engine on the coast. The most advanced instrument in the county is the Assize bell, cast to a pitch that carries over surf, and the second is the tide-slate, a ruled board of black slate on which the day's high water is chalked and which no one is permitted to erase but the Bell-Keeper.
geographies: A drowned coast of mud flats, salt marsh and islands that are only islands twice a day. The Assize causeway runs a mile out from the shore to Gallows Rock and is walkable for about five hours either side of low water. On the rock stand the court, the tide post and the beached hulk of the *Vestry*, a revenue cutter that came ashore ninety years ago and was never floated off. Inland the marsh runs to grazing, and beyond that the county town, which the Assizes visit once and never twice.
races: Bell-Keepers, Circuit Justicars, Marshborn, Shorefolk
civilizations: One county, one court, and a hard division between the people of the shore and the people of the marsh. The shore lives by salvage, oysters and the wrecking trade and considers the law a weather event. The marsh lives by grazing and considers itself the county's conscience. Above both sit the Justicars, appointed for life and travelling in circuit, and beside them the Bell-Keepers -- a guild of one family per coast, who read the water and are the only people whose word can rise a court. Everyone here can tell you how long they have until the water turns.


## Story Details
title: The Salt Assizes
genre: tidal legal mystery
preface: You have rung this court up and down for nineteen years and you have never once been wrong about the water, which is why the chalk on the tide-slate is wrong in somebody else's hand. High water is written as ten minutes past eight. High water is at seven. You wrote seven yourself, last night, on a dry board in a still room, and the figure on the slate now is not yours and is close enough to yours to pass. Out at the post, Neb Halloran has been chained since the ebb for a wrecking nobody on this coast believes he did alone, and his hearing is set for the last hour before the turn -- an hour that, on that chalk, does not exist. The Justicar is already in the court with his gown on. The bell is on its hook. Whoever moved seventy minutes has given the water time to do what the court would have had to sign for.
summary: The player is Coraith Vell, Bell-Keeper of the Assize causeway, who finds the day's high water altered by seventy minutes in a hand that is almost her own. The chained man at the tide post has a hearing in an hour the false chalk has erased, so working out who changed it means reading the court's own papers against the water: the Justicar who needs a verdict, the wreck that serves as the vestry, and the question of who benefits from a drowning the record will call a delay. The tone is cold, procedural and out of doors, and the clock is the sea.


## The Place
name: The Vestry Hulk
teaser: A revenue cutter that came ashore in 1836 and is now where the papers live.

## Instructions
Write this place out in full.
- The description is what the player reads on arrival. Address them as "you"
- Describe what is here now, not the history -- the history is the lore
- Stay consistent with the universe and with the teaser above
- Respect the stated length of each field

## What Is Lying Here
List AT MOST 3 portable things a player could pick up and carry away.
- Nothing is the right answer for most rooms. An empty list is a complete answer
- Only loose, portable things. Not the door, not the floor, not the machinery
  bolted to it -- something a person could put in a pocket or under an arm
- Each one must be consistent with the description you just wrote, and worth
  the player noticing
- Pick its use_kind from the supplied physical profiles. Ordinary is the
  default. Food and drink can be consumed without healing; healing is only
  a restorative dose this world permits. Firestarters burn combustible
  objects, levers pry jammed passages, lockpicks try locks, and a key only
  opens a passage explicitly matched to it. Mark combustible only when an
  ordinary firestarter can destroy the object. The engine owns the effects
  and their amounts; its description cannot grant extra powers
- If a thing has WRITING on it -- a note, a letter, a handbill, a label, a
  docket, a page, a sign -- mark it readable and WRITE OUT WHAT IS WRITTEN
  ON IT, exactly as it appears on the thing. The words themselves, not a
  description of them, and short enough to finish -- a few words, a line,
  or a few short lines. The game keeps those words and a player reading it
  twice reads the same ones
- Never name it after a person or after a place. Already spoken for in this story, so do not reuse: Coraith Vell, Ammon Brace, Neb Halloran, Assize tide-slate

## Who Is Here
Write EXACTLY 3 people who are in this place right now.
- Anyone you write is somebody the player can walk up to and talk to, so they
  have to have a reason to be standing here and something they want
- Do not write the player, and do not write somebody passing through
- Never give them the name of a place, of a thing, or any name already
  spoken for above

Who they are is already decided. Write these people and do not change them:
  the 1st is Marshborn, about 22, female
  the 2nd is Circuit Justicars, about 58, female
  the 3rd is Bell-Keepers, about 26, non-binary

## Their Four Objects of Desire

Write four things this person is after and pick two labels for them. Work from
everything above -- their backstory, what they like and dislike, what they are
afraid of, how old they are, how strong their will is, and where they are
standing.

The two labels are picked from this list and nothing else:

  keep     They are holding on to something they already have.
  obtain   They are trying to get hold of something they do not have.
  reach    They are trying to get to a particular place.
  attend   They are trying to stay near a particular person.
  avoid    They are trying to get away from a person or a place.
  withhold They are trying to stop somebody else getting something.
  offer    They are trying to put something into somebody else's hands.

Rules:
- Every one of the four names something to move TOWARD. A field that only says
  what they want to stop or escape is not finished. Say what is on the other
  side of it.
- Write them so an ordinary act in a room could serve one: picking something
  up, handing something over, walking out, staying put, standing near
  somebody. Do not write a desire nobody could act on in a room.
- Keep them consistent with the fears and dislikes above. A fear is usually the
  shadow of one of these four and should read that way.
- The conscious desire and the unrecognized need must not be the same thing
  said twice.
- Write in the third person, by name.
- Do not resolve any of them, and do not say how the story ends.
- Respect the stated length of each field.
- Each person in this room gets their own four. Two people in one room must not
  want the same thing in the same words.
- At least one of them should want something that is in this room or one step
  out of it.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: The 2 people who are in this place right now. Write all 2 the instructions describe, in the order they are given there.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

unconscious_desire.description: What they are actually pursuing and would deny if you said it to them. It sits at an angle to the conscious desire rather than agreeing with it: the conscious desire is the reason they give themselves, and this is what keeps them going when that reason runs out. One sentence, third person, by name.

A real obligation this world imposes on them -- their work, their family, their debt, their oath, their body -- and one that can get in the way of the conscious desire. One sentence, third person, by name.

unrecognized_need.description: What they need and cannot see, not even unconsciously. A reader should be able to see it from the backstory above while they cannot. need_pursuit.description: Which listed shape the UNRECOGNIZED NEED has. It may be the same label as the one above; the more interesting answer is usually a different one.

detail.description: You stand on the last dry rock of the causeway, where the iron ring is bolted into the stone and the chain runs down to Neb Halloran’s wrist. The tide is still falling, but the air smells of salt and the coming turn. The post itself is a squared pillar of granite, its base ringed with barnacles, and the chain clinks softly against it as the man shifts his weight. A single oil lamp hangs from a hook, its flame steady in the damp wind. The rock is slick with spray, and the horizon is a thin line of darker blue where the water meets the sky.
detail.lore: The Tide Post was set when the *Vestry* grounded, to mark the point where the court’s oaths take hold. The ring and chain are the only restraints the Assizes allow: no irons, no walls, only the certainty that a man chained here cannot walk away from his word once the water hears it. The post has stood through ninety years of storms and hearings, its purpose unchanged, though the rock it stands on is slowly wearing down. The lamp is lit at dusk and extinguished at dawn by whoever is nearest, a duty no one shirks.

prompts.detail:
## Universe Details
physics: Standard physical laws, with one local exception the courts are built around: on this coast an oath spoken over standing salt water binds, and an oath spoken over dry ground does not. Nobody has explained it and everybody has arranged their life around it. A sworn statement made on the causeway at low water holds a man in place -- he cannot walk away from it, cannot contradict it, and will find his own mouth refusing the lie. The same words spoken inland are only words. The binding lasts exactly as long as the water that heard it stays where it is, which on this coast is about six hours.
technology: Sail, tar, oil lamp and iron. Roughly eighteenth century and skewed entirely toward the sea: block and tackle, chain, dredging gear, tide tables computed by hand and reprinted every spring. There is no telegraph and no engine on the coast. The most advanced instrument in the county is the Assize bell, cast to a pitch that carries over surf, and the second is the tide-slate, a ruled board of black slate on which the day's high water is chalked and which no one is permitted to erase but the Bell-Keeper.
geographies: A drowned coast of mud flats, salt marsh and islands that are only islands twice a day. The Assize causeway runs a mile out from the shore to Gallows Rock and is walkable for about five hours either side of low water. On the rock stand the court, the tide post and the beached hulk of the *Vestry*, a revenue cutter that came ashore ninety years ago and was never floated off. Inland the marsh runs to grazing, and beyond that the county town, which the Assizes visit once and never twice.
races: Bell-Keepers, Circuit Justicars, Marshborn, Shorefolk
civilizations: One county, one court, and a hard division between the people of the shore and the people of the marsh. The shore lives by salvage, oysters and the wrecking trade and considers the law a weather event. The marsh lives by grazing and considers itself the county's conscience. Above both sit the Justicars, appointed for life and travelling in circuit, and beside them the Bell-Keepers -- a guild of one family per coast, who read the water and are the only people whose word can rise a court. Everyone here can tell you how long they have until the water turns.


## Story Details
title: The Salt Assizes
genre: tidal legal mystery
preface: You have rung this court up and down for nineteen years and you have never once been wrong about the water, which is why the chalk on the tide-slate is wrong in somebody else's hand. High water is written as ten minutes past eight. High water is at seven. You wrote seven yourself, last night, on a dry board in a still room, and the figure on the slate now is not yours and is close enough to yours to pass. Out at the post, Neb Halloran has been chained since the ebb for a wrecking nobody on this coast believes he did alone, and his hearing is set for the last hour before the turn -- an hour that, on that chalk, does not exist. The Justicar is already in the court with his gown on. The bell is on its hook. Whoever moved seventy minutes has given the water time to do what the court would have had to sign for.
summary: The player is Coraith Vell, Bell-Keeper of the Assize causeway, who finds the day's high water altered by seventy minutes in a hand that is almost her own. The chained man at the tide post has a hearing in an hour the false chalk has erased, so working out who changed it means reading the court's own papers against the water: the Justicar who needs a verdict, the wreck that serves as the vestry, and the question of who benefits from a drowning the record will call a delay. The tone is cold, procedural and out of doors, and the clock is the sea.

The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room". Never the name of the building it is in, never a name this story has already given to a room, a person or a thing, and never a comma.

items.description: Portable things lying loose in this place that a player could pick up and carry away. Empty is the right answer for most rooms.

name.description: What the thing is called, as a player would type it to pick it up. A short noun phrase, 1 to 4 words, lower case unless it is a proper name. Never the name of a person or of a place.

description.description: What it is and what state it is in, consistent with the description of the room you just wrote. One or two sentences.

use_kind.description: The engine's physical profile: ordinary unless it is food, a drink, a healing dose, a firestarter, a prying lever, lockpicks, or a key. Choose healing only for an actual restorative dose allowed by this world. Profiles supply behavior from code, never from the description.

combustible.description: True only if this portable thing can be destroyed by an ordinary carried firestarter: dry paper, cloth or wood. False for stone, metal, liquids, or anything uncertain.

readable.description: True only if this thing has WRITING on it that a player could read: a note, a letter, a label, a docket, a page, a sign, an inscription. False for everything else, which is most things.

inscription.description: The words written on it, exactly as they appear, and only when `readable` is true. Write what is actually on the thing -- what a player would read off it -- not a description of it. A few words, a line, or a few short lines; well under the limit, and finished rather than trailing off. Leave this out entirely when nothing is written on it.

people.description: The 2 people who are in this place right now. Write all 2 the instructions describe, in the order they are given there.

fullname.description: Their full name, as a player would type it to speak to them. 2 or 3 words.

nickname.description: What they are called to their face. 1 or 2 words.

appearance.description: What somebody walking in sees of them, consistent with the room you just wrote and with the race and age you were given for them. One or two sentences.

personality.description: How they behave and how they treat a stranger. One or two sentences.

backstory.description: Why they are in this place and what they want. Third person, by name. Two or three sentences.

likes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they enjoy.

dislikes.description: A comma separated list of 2 or 3 things they cannot stand.

fears.description: A comma separated list of 1 or 2 things they are afraid of.

conscious_desire.description: What this person would say if somebody asked them what they want, today, in this story. Specific, and reachable by somebody standing in a room in this world. Name something to move TOWARD, never something to stop or escape. One sentence, third person, by name.

unconscious_desire.description: What they are actually pursuing and would deny if you said it to them. It sits at an angle to the conscious desire rather than agreeing with it: the conscious desire is the reason they give themselves, and this is what keeps them going when that reason runs out. One sentence, third person, by name.

recognized_need.description: Something they know they must do whether they want to or not, and may resent. A real obligation this world imposes on them -- their work, their family, their debt, their oath, their body -- and one that can get in the way of the conscious desire. One sentence, third person, by name.

history.content:
## Universe Details
physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. The city is divided into districts, each with its unique characteristics, such as the Industrial Quarter, the Residential Loop, and the Sovereign's Circle.
races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Sovereigns live in the opulent Sovereign's Circle, while the rest of the population resides in the ever-changing districts. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. The Verdant Folk live in harmony with nature in the Verdant Expanse, while the Crystal Dwarves mine moonstones in the Crystal Peaks. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.


## Story Details
title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. Your landlord, old Grenn, has left a note under your door demanding the overdue rent by morning, or he'll have your table and your instruments out in the lane by noon. The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.
summary: The player is a cartographer hired by the Lunar Sovereigns to map the nightly rearrangements of the city of Nocturnis, where buildings, streets, and landmarks shift with the moon's phases due to residual magical energy called Nocturna. As they work, they uncover conspiracies within the Sovereigns, encounter the displaced peoples of the Scorch Nomads and Verdant Folk, and grapple with the disorienting effects of prolonged exposure to Nocturna, which causes memory loss. The game's tone is grounded, atmospheric, and focused on mystery and survival in a world that refuses to stay still.

detail.description: The hallway is narrow, its floorboards groaning underfoot as you step onto them, the wood worn smooth by decades of tenants. A single flickering gas lamp casts long, wavering shadows along the peeling floral wallpaper, its pattern faded to a ghost of its former self. The air carries the scent of damp plaster and old varnish, with a faint undercurrent of cabbage from the apartments beyond. A row of mismatched doors lines either side, each marked with a tarnished brass number, their paint chipped and handles slightly loose. At the far end, a narrow staircase spirals upward into dimness, its steps creaking softly as if settling into place for the night.
detail.lore: Grenn's Boarding House was built in the early days after the Great War, when the city's rearrangements were less predictable and survivors sought any shelter they could find. The building has withstood the nightly shifts of Nocturnis for decades, though its walls bear the cracks and scars of constant movement. Grenn Ollivar, a former Scorch Nomad, bought the place years ago and turned it into a boarding house for those who couldn’t afford the stability of the Sovereign’s Circle. The hallway, like the rest of the house, is a testament to the city’s relentless change, its structure bending but never breaking.

physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.

title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. ## Universe Details
physics: This world adheres to standard physical laws, with one exception: the city of Nocturnis, built on the ruins of an ancient war, rearranges itself every night due to the residual magical energy from the Great War. This energy, called Nocturna, is harnessed from the moon and causes buildings, streets, and landmarks to shift and change. The effects of Nocturna are limited to the city boundaries, and its influence wanes during the day, allowing the city to remain static until nightfall. Nocturna does not affect living beings directly, but prolonged exposure can cause disorientation and memory loss. The city's rearrangement follows certain patterns, often influenced by the phases of the moon, but these patterns are complex and not fully understood.
technology: Technology in this world is a blend of pre-war remnants and post-war innovations. The Great War, which ended 75 years ago, left behind advanced but often broken or dangerous technology. The current society has managed to salvage and repurpose some of this tech, but much of it remains beyond their understanding. Most people rely on steam-powered machinery and simple electronics. The city of Nocturnis has a unique technology called Lunar Compasses, which are devices that can predict the city's nightly rearrangements with about 60% accuracy. These compasses are highly sought after but require rare moonstones to function.
geographies: The world is dominated by the ever-changing city of Nocturnis, surrounded by a vast, desolate landscape known as the Scorch. The Scorch is a reminder of the Great War, a wasteland where little life thrives. To the north lies the Crystal Peaks, a mountain range rich in moonstones. To the east, the Verdant Expanse is a vast forest that has begun to reclaim the land. Within Nocturnis, notable landmarks include the Ever-Shifting Bazaar, a marketplace that changes location and layout every night, and the Celestial Spire, a tower that remains static despite the city's rearrangements. The city is divided into districts, each with its unique characteristics, such as the Industrial Quarter, the Residential Loop, and the Sovereign's Circle.
races: Crystal Dwarves, Lunar Sovereigns, Nocturna-Blighted, Scorch Nomads, Verdant Folk
civilizations: The city of Nocturnis is the center of civilization, ruled by the Lunar Sovereigns who control the supply of moonstones and advanced technology. The Sovereigns live in the opulent Sovereign's Circle, while the rest of the population resides in the ever-changing districts. The Scorch Nomads roam the wasteland, trading scavenged pre-war technology and resources with the Verdant Folk and Crystal Dwarves. The Verdant Folk live in harmony with nature in the Verdant Expanse, while the Crystal Dwarves mine moonstones in the Crystal Peaks. Tensions exist between the Lunar Sovereigns and the other factions due to the Sovereigns' control of resources and technology, as well as their secretive and hierarchical nature.


## Story Details
title: The Lunar Cartographer
genre: Fantasy
preface: The apartment smells of boiled cabbage and lamp oil. A fine dust of plaster drifts down from the ceiling where the building groans, settling itself into its new configuration for the night. You sit at the oak table by the window, watching motes swirl in the amber light of your kerosene lamp. Across the scarred wood, a half-finished map of Nocturnis spreads out like a rumor you can't quite believe. The Larkspur Quarter, where you woke this morning, has already migrated two blocks north by your last bearings. The Bell of Saint Aravel chimes once in the distance—11 p.m., or close enough. Outside the open window, the cobblestones of Mournwell Lane breathe with a faint, silvery luminescence, rearranging themselves with the patience of something that has done this for seventy-five years. Your landlord, old Grenn, has left a note under your door demanding the overdue rent by morning, or he'll have your table and your instruments out in the lane by noon. The map is worth more than the rent. Both are due before the city forgets where it put this building.

description.description: What the player sees, hears and smells standing in this place right now. Describe THIS place only -- not what neighbours it, not what is visible out of a window or across the way, because the world around it can move. Second person. One paragraph, 4 to 6 sentences.

lore.description: What this place is, who made it and what happened here. Written for the game engine rather than the player. One paragraph, 3 to 5 sentences.

name.description: What this room is called -- ONLY when the instructions above ask you to name it. Leave this out entirely otherwise. A short noun phrase a player would type to walk into it, carrying the article English wants on it: "the counting room".
